notes.1: Candidates multiplied out the factorised expression and collected like terms well. There were a number of sign slips which resulted in the final quadratic function not always being correct. This was usually factorised to obtain the two critical values. Finding the correct region was not always successful as many seem to just quote the two values found or did not have a strategy to find the values that satisfied the inequality.
notes.4: Only the best candidates could answer this question well. Many did not even attempt it and many others obtained just one mark awarded for changing each term into cos x and sinx . The next step of obtaining a 2 2 quadratic in sinx by using cos x = 1− sin x was a step too far for most who had not tidied up their original expression or not realised that this was the way to proceed. Solving the quadratic and obtaining four values was straightforward for those who got that far.
notes.5: (i) Multiplication of matrices was well understood and candidates only lost the occasional mark by a careless mistake rather than any lack of technique. (ii) Candidates needed to set up two simultaneous equations and solve them. Some candidates wrote down the matrices multiplied by p and q and equated to the identity matrix and did no more. Seeing and choosing two out of four linear equations to solve out of a context that was familiar seemed to be too daunting a task for some. There were a number of fully correct answers. 7 8   1 4   −4 −1 5 5  
notes.6: (i) There were a fair number of candidates who did not respond to this question at all but there were many who recognised that what was required was the number of permutations of 4 items from 5 and got the answer easily. (ii) Many candidates realised that what was required was the number of permutations of 3 out of 4 multiplied by the number of permutations of 2 out of 6. A few thought that the second term was 2 out of 5, not realising that all remaining numbers can be selected for the last two places. (iii) Many realised that the number of ways for first and last was P and the number of ways for the middle three was P . The only issue was those who thought that one was a prime number.
notes.7: (i) The responses to this question fell into three categories in the main. Firstly there were those who were familiar with the requirement, could add fractions, knew their trig identities and scored full marks. Secondly there were those who struggled with the algebra and knew little trig, even ending up inventing identities and scored at most one mark. Finally there were those who realised their limitations and moved on to the next question. 2 2 2 (ii) Candidates used the given expression in order to obtain an equation in tan x ,sin x or cos x and a number then solved to find values of x. Unfortunately, many took only the positive square root and so obtained just two values rather than four.
notes.8: (i) This question was done well only by the better candidates. Of the others there were those who knew that they had to use calculus but did not differentiate well and then there were others who attempted to find the equation by other means. There were a number who did not attempt this part at all. (ii) This part also proved demanding for many of the candidates and a number, once again, made no attempt. Those who did attempt it knew to find the area of the trapezium and then integrate the curve between the given limits. Many did not get the integral correct but did obtain some credit for their other work.
notes.9: (i) Most candidates appreciated that the circumference of the semi-circle was πr and this enabled them to complete this part successfully. (ii) As the answer was given, candidates had to be aware that sufficient working was shown. All those who scored both marks had used their answers to part (i) correctly to find the given area. A few fell short due to insufficient working but on the whole this part was answered well. (iii) This part was found difficult by the average candidate but was done well by those who were aware of what was required and were not put off by the fact that the given function contained π . 5 − 2r − πr
notes.10: (i) Forming a quadratic in x or y and equating the discriminant to zero was the required method in this question. Solutions were often spoilt by careless algebraic and sign errors and some candidates were not aware that dealing with the discriminant was the way forward. (ii) Candidates had to use their values of k in order to establish the point of contact between line and curve. This proved too demanding for those who had not found an integer value of k and many attempts were left incomplete. (iii) There were follow through marks available for those who had found two points in part (ii) and so correct methods were rewarded regardless of previous errors.
notes.11: It was expected that candidates would attempt to fill in the blank regions of the Venn diagram with values in terms of x . This was possible if one started with set H, moved on to set R and finally set N. After this an equation in x could be formed by equating the total to 70. However, this process was adopted by very few. Many introduced other letters for regions which were not always clearly defined and produced a number of equations which were not always of any use.
notes.key_messages: Candidates should be encouraged to attempt all questions. Often, the first mark or two can be earned by making a start at a question even if the candidate is unable to complete it. Candidates need to take care with their algebra to ensure that marks are not lost through careless slips.
notes.general_comments: The quality of presentation has improved this year. There has been less irrelevant working which can lead to confusion to both the candidate themself and the Examiner. Many candidates could show that they had a good grasp of all areas of the syllabus. However, many candidates appeared to have less than a full understanding of all the topic areas. It is important that candidates have covered the whole syllabus.
notes.2a: This was tackled well by many who appeared to have a good grasp of the logarithm law requirements to tackle this question. In fact, those who did not get the final answer correct were often guilty of poor algebra rather than any lack of knowledge of logs.
notes.2b: It was expected that candidates would combine the exponential terms first before taking natural logs as the second step before making y the subject. However many took logs as their first step resulting in the common incorrect statements (1− 2y )ln2e = (3y + 2 ln3e) or 2 1( − 2y) = 3 3( y + 2) .
notes.3a: The vast majority of candidates multiplied the brackets out successfully and completed the rest to get a correct answer. There were relatively few who made sign errors or made mistakes in simplification.
notes.3b: Rationalising the fraction appeared to cause few problems and dealing with the 12 and 18 terms also was done well resulting in many answers gaining full marks.
